fig17_1: Three side-by-side line plots of solution profiles, each showing a deliberate time-stepping blow-up. Left, Fourier advection stepped just above its stability limit, where rapid sawtooth oscillations at the highest wavenumbers have grown to fill the whole domain. Centre, the Chebyshev wave equation with leapfrog at fifty percent too large a step, where the violent oscillations are confined to the two boundaries at x equals plus and minus one. Right, the Chebyshev heat equation with forward Euler at triple the stable step, again erupting near the boundaries. The common lesson: instability first strikes the modes tied to the largest eigenvalues of the spatial operator.
fig17_2: A two-by-three grid plotting, in the complex z-plane with real axis horizontal and imaginary axis vertical, the stability regions of six time integrators with stable interiors shaded. Top row: forward Euler is a unit disk centred at minus one; classical RK4 reaches about two point eight units along both axes; first-order leapfrog is just the open segment of the imaginary axis between minus two i and plus two i. Bottom row: Adams-Bashforth 2 is a small region near the origin; Crank-Nicolson fills the entire left half-plane; backward Euler covers everything outside the unit disk centred at plus one, including the whole left half-plane. The contrast shows explicit methods have small bounded regions while implicit ones are unbounded.
fig17_3: Two panels overlaying scaled eigenvalues, drawn as dots, onto time-integrator stability regions in the complex plane. Left, the RK4 region with the purely imaginary eigenvalues of the Fourier first-derivative matrix for N equals thirty-two at two step sizes: one set sits inside the region (stable), the other spills outside (unstable). Right, the forward Euler unit disk with the real negative eigenvalues of the Chebyshev second-derivative matrix for N equals sixteen, where outlier eigenvalues near minus zero point zero four eight times N to the fourth lie far to the left, forcing an extremely small time step to keep every dot inside the disk.
fig17_4: Two panels. Left, the eigenvalues of the Fourier differentiation matrix for N equals thirty-two plotted in the complex plane, all lying on the imaginary axis between minus sixteen i and plus sixteen i. Right, the critical time step versus N on log-log axes for RK4 applied to Fourier advection with unit speed; the data fall on a straight line of slope minus one, confirming order N to the minus one scaling, with a dashed reference line at two point eight three divided by N over two.
fig17_5: Two panels for variable-coefficient Fourier advection. Left, the speed profile c of x equals one plus one half sine x plotted over the domain, with its maximum value of three halves marked. Right, the critical time step versus N on log-log axes for RK4; the experimental thresholds (markers) converge from below toward a dashed frozen-coefficient prediction two point eight three over the product of c-max and N over two, lying below a dotted constant-coefficient reference line, confirming the frozen-coefficient heuristic for this smooth speed.
fig17_6: Eigenvalues of the Chebyshev second-derivative matrix with Dirichlet boundary conditions for N equals thirty-two, plotted along the real axis, all real and negative. About two over pi of them are physical modes clustering near the exact values minus n squared pi squared over four, marked with circles, while the remaining outlier eigenvalues stretch out to roughly minus zero point zero four eight times N to the fourth, near five times ten to the fourth, far beyond the physical range.
fig17_7: Two panels comparing eigenvectors of the Chebyshev second-derivative matrix for N equals thirty-two. Left, a physical eigenvector (mode eight) oscillating smoothly across the interval and tracking the sine curve sine of eight pi times x plus one over two. Right, the outlier eigenvector belonging to the largest eigenvalue, sharply peaked at the boundaries x equals plus and minus one and decaying rapidly into the interior. This boundary-localised, physically meaningless mode is what dictates the explicit time-step limit.
fig17_8: Log-log plot of the spectral radius of the Chebyshev second-derivative matrix versus N. The data fall on a straight line of slope four, confirming order N to the fourth growth, with a dashed fitted line at zero point zero four eight times N to the fourth lying on top of the points.
fig17_9: Two panels of pseudospectral contours in the complex plane for two operators sharing the same eigenvalues minus one through minus N, shown as dots. Left, a normal diagonal operator, where the contours are tight concentric disks hugging each eigenvalue. Right, a highly nonnormal upper-triangular operator, where the contours balloon far beyond the eigenvalues and reach into the right half-plane, signalling possible large transient growth even though every eigenvalue is stable. Contour levels are the base-ten logarithm of one over epsilon for epsilon equal to ten to the minus one, ten to the minus two, and so on.
fig17_10: Two panels comparing six time-stepping strategies for the Fourier heat equation at N equals sixty-four and viscosity zero point one. Left, error versus time step on log-log axes: forward Euler is confined to very small steps by the CFL limit, while Crank-Nicolson and the integrating-factor method reach far smaller errors at much larger steps. Right, error versus wall-clock time, exposing the efficiency trade-off, where IF-RK4 and Crank-Nicolson dominate, attaining near machine-precision accuracy at modest cost.
tbl17_1: Table summarizing six time-stepping strategies for diffusive problems, listing each method's order, stable time-step (CFL) limit for the Fourier heat equation, whether it is implicit, and its main cost, showing that unconditionally stable implicit and exponential methods trade a per-step price for freedom from the explicit step restriction.
fig17_11: Two panels comparing plain RK4 against integrating-factor RK4 for the KdV equation. Left, the maximum admissible time step versus N: plain RK4 (circles) falls off as N to the minus three because of the i k cubed dispersion, while IF-RK4 (squares) is limited only by the mild nonlinearity and declines far more gently. Right, the solution at time one for N equals one hundred twenty-eight, where both methods agree to graphical accuracy, but IF-RK4 reaches that time in about one hundred steps versus roughly ten thousand for plain RK4.
tbl17_2: Table summarizing the seven computational etudes of the chapter, giving each one's topic, key insight, and the relevant time-step scaling law, from the visual catastrophe gallery through Fourier order N to the minus one and Chebyshev order N to the minus four restrictions to the roughly hundredfold speedup of integrating-factor RK4 on KdV.
